lines.text: So far we priced what one algorithm costs. A lower bound asks the opposite: what must every algorithm pay?

Take a million keys and three colleagues, who may only compare keys. One promises to sort any input in fifteen million comparisons. One promises to find the smallest and largest in one point two million. One promises to decide whether all keys differ in five million.
You cannot test your way to a refutation, because you would have to find the bad input first.
So we will use an adversary instead, and refute all three without running a single program.
If the only thing an algorithm may do is compare, then everything it learns is a string of yes or no answers.
Draw every possible string for three keys and you get a binary tree. Each internal node is one comparison; each leaf is a finished run that reports one ordering.
How much a given input costs is how deep its leaf sits. The worst case is the height of the tree.
Notice the unit has changed. We now count comparisons, not word operations, and everything else is free, so a lower bound here limits time from below only; it can never serve as an upper bound.
Three keys can arrive in six different orders.
Think about what two comparisons can distinguish. Can any comparison sort finish every input of three keys with just two?
No. Some input needs three.
Two yes or no answers give four outcomes, so a tree of height two has at most four leaves, but six orders need six.
Another way to say it: an adversary always keeps the bigger half of the orders alive, and two orders are still alive after two comparisons. Three do suffice, as insertion sort's tree shows.
Generalise the counting. A correct sort must be able to produce every one of the n factorial orders, so its tree needs at least that many leaves.
A tree of height h has at most two to the h leaves. So the height is at least log of n factorial, and that is order n log n.
Try it on five keys. There are a hundred and twenty orders, between sixty four and a hundred and twenty eight, so seven comparisons are unavoidable.
For a million keys, some input costs at least eighteen and a half million.
The worst case of merge sort is only two point five percent above that.
The upper bound and the lower bound meet. Sorting by comparison is settled.

lines.text: The bound holds on average too.
With every order equally likely, any comparison sort's average leaf depth is at least the floor of log base two of n factorial. A sharper count even removes the floor.
The proof is the move you just watched. Hang the two deepest sibling leaves under the shallowest leaf, and the average drops.
So the cheapest tree is balanced, and luck does not help on average.
Look at what the argument actually used. Nothing about sorting, only the number of possible answers.
With K answers you need at least log base two of K yes or no questions, rounded up, whatever those questions are.

Try it. Searching the sorted vector has a million and one answers, so twenty questions, and binary search uses exactly twenty. Merging two runs of four has seventy interleavings, so seven, and the standard merge meets it. Sorting five keys: seven again.
In these cases counting is tight. Hold that thought, because the next case will break it.
Finding the largest of a million keys has a million answers. Counting says twenty questions.
Before you trust that, ask what a comparison can tell you. It names a winner and a loser. How many comparisons must every comparison algorithm make in the worst case?
Nine hundred and ninety nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety nine.
A key might still be the largest until it has lost once. So all keys but one must lose, and each comparison produces just one loser.
Counting gave a true bound, but a very weak one: twenty free-form questions could find the maximum, but a comparison is not allowed to ask them.
That was an adversary argument. Its answers pretended that each key's value was its own number.
The adversary answers each comparison as it likes, with one rule. The answers so far must always fit some real input.
It assumes nothing about the algorithm, so it covers every algorithm at once.
Here, a tournament stops after six comparisons. Two keys were never beaten.
Raise one of them, and every answer still holds... but the maximum changes.
The algorithm cannot tell the two inputs apart. It is wrong on one of them.
Two scans find the largest and then the smallest of the rest in seven plus six, thirteen comparisons. That is an upper bound.
Can you do better? What is the fewest comparisons any algorithm can guarantee on eight keys?
Ten.
Pair the keys up first, four comparisons. The largest can only be a winner of a pair, and the smallest only a loser, so three more comparisons each.
Four plus three plus three makes ten. The next step shows that nobody can guarantee nine.
Now the referee keeps a scoreboard, with four columns.
Until a key has lost, it could be the maximum. Until it has won, it could be the minimum.
So a correct answer needs fourteen units: every key but the maximum must lose once, and every key but the minimum must win once.

Only a comparison of two untested keys gives two units, and there are at most four of those. The referee answers every other comparison so that it gives at most one. A key that only won always beats a key that only lost, for nothing.
Watch the units climb to fourteen, while the comparisons stop at ten.
So every algorithm needs at least three n over two, minus two.
Pairing meets it.
For a million keys, about one and a half million.
Now a yes or no question: are all the keys distinct? Counting gives two answers, so one question.
But be careful. What must a comparison algorithm pay on a million keys in the worst case?
About eighteen and a half million.
The answer has two values, but the knowledge behind it is large. To say distinct safely, the algorithm must effectively learn the whole sorted order, so it pays the sorting bound.
One question is the counting bound: true, and useless here.
Suppose an algorithm says distinct, without ever comparing two keys that are neighbors in sorted order.
Nothing lies between them, so the adversary makes them equal.
Every answer stays the same. The algorithm still says distinct... and now it is wrong.
So every distinct answer rests on all the neighbor comparisons. Together they spell out the whole sorted order.
The tree needs at least n factorial leaves, and the sorting bound applies.
It even survives a stronger model, algebraic computation trees, which may also add, multiply, divide and take square roots.
A lower bound is a precise statement, so be precise about what it excludes. Nothing more.
It covers one model: only comparisons reveal anything about the keys. And one problem: output the sorted order of any input.

So it leaves radix sort alone, which reads digits. It leaves hash sets alone, which compute on the bits and promise only expected linear time. It leaves fast cases alone, and different problems such as the smallest half first, and better constants.
And it is not the cost of any one algorithm: insertion sort's quadratic count is its own.
The practical lesson: to beat a bound, change something it assumed.

lines.text: Return to the three promises. None can be kept by a comparison algorithm, and you showed it without running anything.
The sort needed a tree with n factorial leaves. The minimum and maximum needed a scoreboard of units. The distinctness check needed a neighbour argument.
Escape is possible by using the keys as numbers: sort digit by digit and scan for equal neighbours. But for minimum and maximum, pairing is the best any comparison algorithm can do.
One more observation. Everything so far priced one run on its worst input. A data structure lives through a whole sequence of operations, and that is the next reel.

lines.text: Merge two sorted runs of eight keys each. There are twelve thousand, eight hundred and seventy ways they can interleave, and counting gives fourteen comparisons.
Is that enough? What must every merge pay in the worst case?
Fifteen.
Let one run hold the odd numbers and the other the even ones. In the merged order, every neighbouring pair comes from different runs.
Only a direct comparison can separate those neighbours, so all fifteen must be compared. The adversary beat counting by one.

lines.text: A student's adversary for the maximum answers every comparison the same way: the first key named is larger.
Does that prove it?
Does every algorithm need one fewer than n comparisons?
No. Its answers can fit no input.
Ask a against b, b against c, then c against a. It says a beats b beats c beats a. No input fits that.
So the run it forces is not a run on any input, and it proves nothing.
An adversary may decide late, but never inconsistently.
Which of these claims about a million keys does the comparison sorting lower bound refute?
The comparison sort that averages seventeen million.
The average cost is at least about eighteen point five million comparisons.
Radix sort is outside the model. A sorted input is one easy input. And the ten largest is a different problem.
